newsitem.title: USA: Pilots near labor accord with American.
newsitem.headline: Pilots near labor accord with American.

text.p: Negotiators for the pilots union at American Airlines and for the airline reached a tentative agreement on a new contract, spokesmen for both sides said on Wednesday, raising hopes for an end to their labor dispute.
"We are pleased to have a deal. While it does not give us all we had hoped for, we very much wanted to resolve this matter," American Airlines President Donald Carty said in a written statement.
The company declined to provide any details of the pact, pending ratification by the union board and membership.

A spokesman for the 9,300-member Allied Pilots Association (APA) at first termed the development a "tentative agreement," but later backed away, saying it could not be tentative until approved by the board and the union's members. He would not comment further.

If board members approve any offer when they meet on Friday, it will be sent to union members for ratification. But the members could rebuff the board. The board last August voted 10-8 to approve a tentative contract, but when taken to the pilots, 61 percent of them turned it down.

The developments on Wednesday came after a day of talks in Washington and weekend talks near Seattle that were overseen by Robert Harris, chairman of the emergency board created by President Bill Clinton last month to try to resolve the dispute.
Clinton formed the Presidential Emergency Board (PEB) after earlier talks collapsed and the pilots went on strike.

At issue between the nation's No. 2 airline and the APA are a pay raise and whether APA pilots will fly new, small jets American plans to buy for its American Eagle commuter airline or whether Eagle pilots will fly them. Eagle pilots are represented by another union.
The action came as the PEB sent its suggestions for a new labor contract to Clinton and the pilots and the airlines.

Included in the board's recommendations were pay raises for the pilots totaling 6.5 percent from 1997 throgh 2000 along with stock options to resolve their salary concerns, the White House said in a statement.
The union has asked for an 11 percent pay raise to cover the past three years when it had no increase and the next four. American had offered 6.5 percent.
The PEB also said that while not recommending that regional jets be flown by APA pilots, restrictions should be put on the use of them to add to the job security of APA pilots.
The APA wanted its pilots, who earn an average of $120,000 a year, to fly the regional jets, but American wanted them flown by its Eagle pilots, whose pay is about $35,000 a year.
The union was concerned that American might use the regional jets, with ranges of up to 1,000 miles, to fly routes now flown by American planes piloted by APA members.
It was not clear whether any of these recommendations would be part of the offer to be taken to the union's board.
Clinton created the board on Feb. 15, minutes after five days of round-the-clock talks between American and the union broke down and the pilots went out on strike.

Under terms of the law invoked to create the PEB, the pilots were required to go back to work for 30 days while the board fashioned a proposed settlement and remain on the job for another 30 while the two sides considered whether or not to accept it.
The "cooling off" period has been extended to April 28, when the union will be free to strike.
Then, only Congress could end a strike, by passing legislation to send the pilots back to work and to require them to accept the PEB's recommended settlement or to accept binding arbitration.
